highlights.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. highlights.content: [![UF Monogram logo](/media/templates/mercury-10/img/MercuryLogo-OrangeBlock.svg "school-logo") News](/) School Logo Link [University of Florida](https://www.ufl.edu) For Faculty * [Faculty Resources](/for-faculty/) * [Senior Communicators](/for-faculty/senior-communicators/) For Media * [Contact](/for-media/contact/) * [Subscribe to UF News Releases](/for-media/subscribe-to-uf-news-releases/) * [UF Facts for Media](/for-media/uf-facts/) * [UF Administration](https://www.ufl.edu/about/administration/) * [UF Directory](https://search.ufl.edu/) * [Hurricane Hub](https://experts.ufl.edu/hurricanes/) # Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue Harrem Monkhorst Share * Sumit Jha, Ph.D., has developed a system designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue. * His ATLAS system scans an LLM and senses when the model begins to drift from the task and redirects. * The system works inside AI models and does not impact speed or performance. As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their designated tasks is a growing challenge.  University of Florida computer science professor [Sumit Jha, Ph.D.](https://cise.ufl.edu/people/faculty/name/sumit-jha/), is working to keep agents from “going rogue.” Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands.   The research comes as news reports have chronicled AI agents gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder.  Jha, a professor in UF’s Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or [CISE](https://cise.ufl.edu/), studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, non-invasive tweaks to keep systems on task. > “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.” —Sumit Jha, Ph.D., professor, UF Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper entitled “Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI,” detailing a system, dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory.  The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system.  Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it self-generates. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information.    “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong,” Jha explained. “Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.”   Existing strategies usually involve policing an AI agent’s answers after the fact. The ATLAS system doesn’t require retraining the model, and it therefore doesn’t expend extra computing resources or slow the model down.   According to Jha, so-called task drift is especially possible for tasks in which groups of AI agents coordinate with each other over long periods of time.  “Say, initially you told the agent you’re a doctor, you are supposed to treat patients,” Jha said. “By day No. 7, the fact that it's a doctor and it should treat patients is now just one of the millions of things it ...

As their leadership philosophies become embedded in business operations, founder-led companies can develop distinct competitive advantages that support sustainable growth. Currently, approximately 11% of large-cap U.S. companies are founder-led. Despite accounting for less than 5% of the S&P 500, founder-led businesses wield considerable influence over the broader market. Visionary entrepreneurs such as Elon Musk, Warren Buffett, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates have reshaped industries and built globally recognized enterprises. highlights.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. highlights.content: ![The Motley Fool](https://g.foolcdn.com/misc-assets/logo-tmf-primary-1-magenta-purple-reversed.svg?_w=320) ![The Motley Fool](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Fmisc-assets%2Ftmf_holdingco_logo_stacked_magenta_royalpurple_rev.png&w=96&op=resize) **Nvidia** ([NVDA](/quote/nasdaq/nvda/) -1.05%) and **Advanced Micro Devices** ([AMD](/quote/nasdaq/amd/) -2.41%) are two of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. As big tech [invests hundreds of billions of dollars in data centers](https://www.fool.com/research/ai-companies-spending-on-data-centers/), demand for semiconductors continues to accelerate. However, another chipmaker could deliver even greater returns over the next several years: **Marvell Technology** ([MRVL](/quote/nasdaq/mrvl/) -14.29%). Interestingly, Nvidia CEO [Jensen Huang](https://www.fool.com/investing/how-to-invest/famous-investors/jensen-huang/) recognizes Marvell's potential. During the Computex conference in June, Huang called Marvell the next potential trillion-dollar company. Nvidia has even invested $2 billion in Marvell, reinforcing its confidence in the company. Now, Marvell is reportedly exploring an acquisition that could supercharge its position in the AI infrastructure market. Let's dig into what makes Marvell unique and assess why the stock could be a compelling buy for long-term investors. ![Marvell logo.](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Feditorial%2Fimages%2F892727%2Fmrvl.jpg&w=3840&op=resize) Image source: The Motley Fool. ## What role does Marvell play in the AI chip stack? Nvidia and AMD primarily design general-purpose AI accelerators, known as GPUs. Marvell specializes in designing [custom application-specific integrated circuits](https://www.fool.com/terms/a/application-specific-integrated-circuit/) (ASICs). These processors are tailored to specific workloads, potentially offering superior training and inference performance, energy efficiency, and economics compared with off-the-shelf chips. This value proposition appeals to hyperscalers such as **Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms**. Rather than relying exclusively on products from Nvidia and AMD, big tech is also investing in custom silicon designed around their own AI models. Marvell is positioning itself as a partner in this transition. Marvell's opportunity extends beyond custom chips. Its portfolio also includes optical digital signal processors (DSPs)**,** Ethernet switches, high-speed interconnects, and silicon photonics. These products help move data between larger clusters of GPUs and memory. As AI models evolve and use cases become more sophisticated, Marvell's services should see increased demand. ## Is Marvell acquiring Lumentum? On Oct. 28, Reuters reported that Marvell was in advanced discussions to acquire **Lumentum** ([LITE](/quote/nasdaq/lite/) +0.79%), a manufacturer of optical components used in telecommunications networks and AI data centers. Wall Street initially reacted negatively, as Marvell stock declined more than 8% following reports of the discussions. ## [MRVL](/quote/nasdaq/mrvl/) - Marvell Technology NASDAQ · As of 3:35 PM ET 10/29/26 ![](/jester-cap-color.svg) ### Key data points The concerns are understandable. At the end of its fiscal second quarter, Marvell held approximately $3.9 billion in cash on its balance sheet. Lumentum boasts a market capitalization of $84 billion, meaning that an acquisition of this magnitude would require substantial borrowing, additional share issuance, or some combination of both by Marvell. Even so, I see the strategic rationale here. One challenge facing AI data centers is moving information quickly and efficiently between large clusters of processors. Copper-based connections have limitations around bandwidth, distance, and power consumption. highlights.content: SecurityBrief Australia - Technology news for CISOs & cybersecurity decision-makers [![SecurityBrief Australia logo](/brands/sb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![CrowdStrike uncovers China-linked AI cyber campaign](https://securitybrief.com.au/uploads/story/2026/10/30/global-network-map-central-hub-intrusion-arrows-office-buildings-data-centers-story-323039.webp) [AI](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/artificial-intelligence) [Cybersecurity](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/cybersecurity) [Agentic AI](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/ai-agents) # CrowdStrike uncovers China-linked AI cyber campaign Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://securitybrief.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) CrowdStrike has uncovered a cyber espionage campaign by China-linked threat actor VAPOR PANDA, which used an agentic artificial intelligence framework to conduct simultaneous intrusions against more than 200 organisations worldwide. The campaign began on October 17, 2026, and involved ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI framework, alongside the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model (LLM) and a second commercial LLM. The operation targeted government institutions, pharmaceutical companies, semiconductor organisations, defence entities and telecommunications providers. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller directed against organisations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day period. The activity included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as US-based organisations in several strategic industries. The cybersecurity company confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organisations, where the attackers gained access, deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and conducted further credential spraying, network scanning and reconnaissance. At least 12 additional organisations were subjected to password-spraying and credential-scanning activity, including US think tanks and European government entities. **Broad targeting** VAPOR PANDA conducted extensive intrusions against foreign ministries in two Latin American countries and likely compromised a third. The group also prepared target files for foreign ministries in Central America and Asia. In the Middle East, the adversary compromised an interior ministry. Another operation focused on a European country, targeting its foreign ministry, presidency and prime minister's office, alongside defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities. The campaign also involved 19 US-based organisations across the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defence, nuclear and financial sectors. Telecommunications providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also compromised. The targeting represents an expansion of VAPOR PANDA's previous activities. highlights.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Compact audio-visual AI reads sentiment from live video with 84.89% accuracy ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Compact audio-visual AI reads sentiment from live video with 84.89% accuracy](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-21882-750x422.png) Compact audio-visual AI reads sentiment from live video with 84.89% accuracy A team of researchers in Thailand and Japan has built a compact neural network that reads a person’s sentiment from live video streams by combining facial expressions and speech, achieving 84.89 percent accuracy on a three-class task while using roughly ten times fewer parameters than comparable audio-visual systems. The work, published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, also benchmarks nine large language models on the same problem and finds they fall well short of the specialized model when audio and visual information must be interpreted together. The framework, developed by Atitaya Yakaew and Matthew N. Dailey at the Asian Institute of Technology together with Teeradaj Racharak and Watanee Jearanaiwongkul at Tohoku University, classifies affective states as negative, neutral, or positive. It was designed from the outset for low-latency operation on continuous video, the kind of feed produced by cameras already installed in retail and service environments. The authors argue that such streams are a largely under-used resource for understanding customer reactions, since they capture facial expressions and speech simultaneously without requiring people to fill in questionnaires or take part in focus groups. Architecturally, the system consists of four lightweight deep neural networks. A face and mouth detection stage uses a histogram-of-oriented-gradients detector with a linear support vector machine, together with dlib’s facial landmark detector, to crop each face to 96 by 96 pixels and each mouth region to 28 by 28 pixels from frames extracted every 35 milliseconds. A small five-layer convolutional network then classifies each mouth as open or closed, thresholding the predicted probability of an open mouth at 0.5. This mouth-state gate is the distinctive feature of the design: when the mouth is closed across a buffered sequence of ten frames, only the visual pathway runs; when the mouth is open in any frame, audio enters the pipeline. In the audio-visual branch, speech segments are transformed in real time with a short-time Fourier transform into spectrogram images of 400 by 400 pixels, using a 256-sample window, a hop size of six samples at a 48 kHz sampling rate, and a Tukey window, yielding 129 frequency bins rendered on a decibel scale. Parallel convolutional neural network and long short-term memory, or LSTM, branches process the face-image and spectrogram sequences, each with nine convolutional layers, three pooling layers, batch normalization, and an LSTM layer with 20 percent dropout. The two representations are concatenated and passed to a softmax layer over the three sentiment classes. Predictions from the tenth frame of each face track onward are averaged to produce a single sentiment label for the track. The entire architecture contains 20,897,598 trainable parameters. The researchers trained and evaluated the system on the Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech, or RAVDESS, which contains 24 professional actors speaking with a neutral North American accent. Because categories such as surprise, disgust, and fear have valence that shifts with context, the team grouped the eight emotion labels into three sentiment classes: calm and neutral became neutral, happy became positive, and angry and sad became negative. AI Agents.content: [![UF Monogram logo](/media/templates/mercury-10/img/MercuryLogo-OrangeBlock.svg "school-logo") News](/) School Logo Link [University of Florida](https://www.ufl.edu) For Faculty * [Faculty Resources](/for-faculty/) * [Senior Communicators](/for-faculty/senior-communicators/) For Media * [Contact](/for-media/contact/) * [Subscribe to UF News Releases](/for-media/subscribe-to-uf-news-releases/) * [UF Facts for Media](/for-media/uf-facts/) * [UF Administration](https://www.ufl.edu/about/administration/) * [UF Directory](https://search.ufl.edu/) * [Hurricane Hub](https://experts.ufl.edu/hurricanes/) # Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue Harrem Monkhorst Share * Sumit Jha, Ph.D., has developed a system designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue. * His ATLAS system scans an LLM and senses when the model begins to drift from the task and redirects. * The system works inside AI models and does not impact speed or performance. As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their designated tasks is a growing challenge.  University of Florida computer science professor [Sumit Jha, Ph.D.](https://cise.ufl.edu/people/faculty/name/sumit-jha/), is working to keep agents from “going rogue.” Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands.   The research comes as news reports have chronicled AI agents gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder.  Jha, a professor in UF’s Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or [CISE](https://cise.ufl.edu/), studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, non-invasive tweaks to keep systems on task. > “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.” —Sumit Jha, Ph.D., professor, UF Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper entitled “Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI,” detailing a system, dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory.  The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system.  Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it self-generates. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information.    “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong,” Jha explained. “Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.”   Existing strategies usually involve policing an AI agent’s answers after the fact. The ATLAS system doesn’t require retraining the model, and it therefore doesn’t expend extra computing resources or slow the model down.   According to Jha, so-called task drift is especially possible for tasks in which groups of AI agents coordinate with each other over long periods of time.  “Say, initially you told the agent you’re a doctor, you are supposed to treat patients,” Jha said. “By day No. 7, the fact that it's a doctor and it should treat patients is now just one of the millions of things it ...

OpenAI updates AI behavior rules with focus on human intent — Channel NewsAsia [Fedir Kryshtovskyi](/en/%D0%A4%D0%B5%D0%B4%D1%96%D1%80%20%D0%9A%D1%80%D0%B8%D1%88%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B2%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9) 29 October 2026 21:03 ![OpenAI updates AI behavior rules with focus on human intent — Channel NewsAsia](https://cdn-cabinet.ua.news/uploads/images/openai_updated_ai_model_rules_human_inte_1793300625901.webp?8073772 "OpenAI updates AI behavior rules with focus on human intent — Channel NewsAsia") OpenAI has updated its public Model Spec document, which defines the desired principles of behavior for its artificial intelligence models. The new framework is built around five values: fidelity to human intent, minimizing harm, honesty and transparency, human autonomy, and care. ## Human intent as the foundation As [Channel NewsAsia reports](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/business/openai-says-human-intent-center-updated-ai-model-guidelines-6504786), OpenAI called fidelity to human intent the foundation of its new approach. The company believes that models should understand what users, developers, and OpenAI itself seek and value, rather than merely follow instructions literally. The update is part of the company’s work to align AI behavior with human values. According to OpenAI’s plan, models should apply these principles in unfamiliar situations while remaining under human control. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel [Telegram](https://telegram.me/uanewsstream). ## Transparency and user control The revised specification provides that models should reduce potential harm, communicate transparently about what they know and do not know, and help users make their own decisions and achieve their own goals. OpenAI said that current models do not yet fully comply with the updated principles. The company is studying new training methods that could help models learn these rules. The approach resembles Anthropic’s Constitutional AI, where model behavior is guided by a written set of principles. The update was released amid heightened attention to AI alignment after OpenAI reported that an autonomous AI agent hacked Hugging Face during testing. According to the company, the incident showed how advanced models can break rules or bypass safeguards while carrying out assigned tasks. Image by Tim Sandle Artificial intelligence has already changed how many people research a holiday or business trip. The next change could be considerably more disruptive. Rather than simply suggesting a destination, comparing hotels or constructing an itinerary, AI agents are beginning to move closer to carrying out tasks for travellers. This creates a very different technological challenge: an AI system that understands what somebody wants still needs access to the reservation, payment, identity and entitlement systems required to make it happen. The development potentially changes where competitive advantage lies in digital travel. Companies have spent years encouraging consumers to download individual apps and remain within their proprietary ecosystems. An agentic model could instead place a traveller’s preferred AI assistant between the consumer and the travel company. This matters because the industry is already seeing AI alter the discovery process. [Recent reporting by Digital Journal](https://www.digitaljournal.com/article/why-were-starting-to-ask-ai-why-we-should-not-travel/) found research suggesting travellers are employing AI not simply for recommendations but to eliminate destinations from consideration. The article also noted Expedia Group research indicating that travellers were more comfortable using AI for research and recommendations than allowing it to make purchases for them.  Closing that gap between advice and action is where the next technological battle is emerging. The underlying distinction is between generative AI and agentic AI. A conventional AI travel assistant can answer a question such as: “Where should I stay in Barcelona?” An agent needs to go further. It must potentially interact with external software, work through a series of tasks and take authorised actions. This greater autonomy increases the importance of the infrastructure surrounding the model. Evidence from other sectors illustrates that point. [Recent enterprise research reported by Digital Journal](https://www.digitaljournal.com/article/three-in-four-large-enterprises-have-rolled-back-ai-agents/) found organisations had encountered significant difficulties after putting customer-facing agents into production, including data exposure, hallucination or brand risk and difficulties diagnosing failures. Travel adds another layer of complexity. A single journey can involve an airline, hotel, airport, ground transport provider, lounge operator, payment service and loyalty programme, each with its own data and rules. According to Dragonpass, the result is a fragmented environment of APIs, booking engines and separate commercial relationships. An AI assistant might therefore be capable of arranging one element of a journey while being unable to transact with another. ## **The plumbing becomes the product** One technology attracting attention in this context is Model Context Protocol (MCP), which provides a mechanism through which AI applications can interact with external tools and data. Yet technical connectivity alone is not enough. Recent developments ar...

Wiz increasingly sees intrusions where AI agents appear to handle much of the hands-on work and potentially orchestrate the attack itself. These agents operate through harnesses that write custom tooling, inspect the results, adapt, and iterate at machine speed, while a human sets the objectives and guardrails. These attacks can be verbose, with agents trying multiple approaches in parallel. They appear at both ends of the spectrum, from sharply targeted to broadly opportunistic. AI agents compress the skilled, hands-on work that such escalation once required. There is, however, a potential advantage for defenders. ITMO-Developed AI Agent Connects Publications, Authors, and Code Researchers at ITMO’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence have developed [PAUK](https://itmo-nss-team.github.io/PAUK/?tab=1) – the nation’s first open-source software that builds an interactive research connections map using a multi-source dataset: research organizations, employees and their publications, and code repositories. The service works as both a search engine and a map: users can find similar and related developments, authors, researchers, papers, and repositories based on a single article. The project was presented at the 22nd Conference of Open Source Developers in Pereslavl-Zalessky. ![](/images/news/big/p15089.jpg) Credit: SeventyFour / photogenica.ru Researchers use neural networks and software for multiple tasks; they often turn their calculations into code so that their colleagues can use them, too. For that reason, code is just as much a a result of research as the paper itself. However, unlike with publications, finding a piece of code and its author can be a hurdle since repositories may be published privately, links get distorted, and names differ. Because of that, when looking for a particular tool or a collaborator, researchers have to manually look through publications, contact various departments and organizations, or use neural networks. LLMs.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Compact audio-visual AI reads sentiment from live video with 84.89% accuracy ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Compact audio-visual AI reads sentiment from live video with 84.89% accuracy](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-21882-750x422.png) Compact audio-visual AI reads sentiment from live video with 84.89% accuracy A team of researchers in Thailand and Japan has built a compact neural network that reads a person’s sentiment from live video streams by combining facial expressions and speech, achieving 84.89 percent accuracy on a three-class task while using roughly ten times fewer parameters than comparable audio-visual systems. The work, published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, also benchmarks nine large language models on the same problem and finds they fall well short of the specialized model when audio and visual information must be interpreted together. The framework, developed by Atitaya Yakaew and Matthew N. Dailey at the Asian Institute of Technology together with Teeradaj Racharak and Watanee Jearanaiwongkul at Tohoku University, classifies affective states as negative, neutral, or positive. It was designed from the outset for low-latency operation on continuous video, the kind of feed produced by cameras already installed in retail and service environments. The authors argue that such streams are a largely under-used resource for understanding customer reactions, since they capture facial expressions and speech simultaneously without requiring people to fill in questionnaires or take part in focus groups. Architecturally, the system consists of four lightweight deep neural networks. A face and mouth detection stage uses a histogram-of-oriented-gradients detector with a linear support vector machine, together with dlib’s facial landmark detector, to crop each face to 96 by 96 pixels and each mouth region to 28 by 28 pixels from frames extracted every 35 milliseconds. A small five-layer convolutional network then classifies each mouth as open or closed, thresholding the predicted probability of an open mouth at 0.5. This mouth-state gate is the distinctive feature of the design: when the mouth is closed across a buffered sequence of ten frames, only the visual pathway runs; when the mouth is open in any frame, audio enters the pipeline. In the audio-visual branch, speech segments are transformed in real time with a short-time Fourier transform into spectrogram images of 400 by 400 pixels, using a 256-sample window, a hop size of six samples at a 48 kHz sampling rate, and a Tukey window, yielding 129 frequency bins rendered on a decibel scale. Parallel convolutional neural network and long short-term memory, or LSTM, branches process the face-image and spectrogram sequences, each with nine convolutional layers, three pooling layers, batch normalization, and an LSTM layer with 20 percent dropout. The two representations are concatenated and passed to a softmax layer over the three sentiment classes. Predictions from the tenth frame of each face track onward are averaged to produce a single sentiment label for the track. The entire architecture contains 20,897,598 trainable parameters. The researchers trained and evaluated the system on the Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech, or RAVDESS, which contains 24 professional actors speaking with a neutral North American accent. Because categories such as surprise, disgust, and fear have valence that shifts with context, the team grouped the eight emotion labels into three sentiment classes: calm and neutral became neutral, happy became positive, and angry and sad became negative. Each entire video received a single clip-level label, a choice the authors acknowledge introduces label noise when a clip contains segment...

LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Consistency Is Not Correctness: LLM Output Stability Fails to Predict Extraction Accuracy ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Consistency Is Not Correctness: LLM Output Stability Fails to Predict Extraction Accuracy](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-23874-750x422.png) Consistency Is Not Correctness: LLM Output Stability Fails to Predict Extraction Accuracy Large language models asked to pull structured facts out of scientific text can repeat themselves confidently and still be wrong. That is the uncomfortable conclusion of a systematic evaluation in which four widely used generative models—GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, the Moonshot model Kimi, and Qwen3 in non-thinking mode—were repeatedly prompted, without any fine-tuning, to extract entities and relations from a demanding plant-health dataset. The study, published in Genomics & Informatics, measured how often each model produced the same answers across repeated runs and compared that stability, called consistency, against how often the answers were actually correct. The correlation between the two turned out to be weak across every model tested. The researchers framed their work around a practical question. Self-consistency techniques, which generate several outputs from the same prompt and pick the most frequent one, rest on the assumption that a model that agrees with itself is probably right. If that assumption held, consistency could serve as a cheap, model-agnostic filter: run the model a few times, keep only the predictions that recur, and discard the rest. Earlier work had offered encouraging hints, with one prominent study arguing that consistency is almost correctness, because stable outputs more often than not reflect accurate patterns learned from training data. But the assumption is not guaranteed—a model can be consistently and confidently wrong—and whether it holds for structured information extraction had remained largely untested. To test it properly, the team needed a task where correctness is unambiguous and difficulty is real. They chose document-level relation extraction on the EPOP corpus, a dataset built for the epidemiomonitoring of plants. EPOP comes with a rich annotation schema: originally seven named entity types and seven binary relation types with strict constraints on which entity classes can serve as the source and target of each relation. For the experiments the authors focused on five entity types and five relation types. The corpus includes nested and discontinuous entities, synonyms, abbreviations and acronyms, and both short and long-distance overlapping relations, making it a genuinely hard benchmark rather than a toy problem. The experimental design deliberately isolated inference-time behavior. The models were used in a hard-prompting, zero-shot setting: no fine-tuning, just a carefully crafted instruction asking each model to identify the entities in a document and return the relations between them as triplets of source, relation type, and target, formatted as JSON. Document-level extraction was chosen over text-bound extraction partly because it collapses into a single generation step, and partly because generative models struggle to pinpoint exact character offsets in text. Interestingly, asking the models to perform named entity recognition as an intermediate step before relation extraction measurably improved both the accuracy and the consistency of their relation predictions compared with asking for relations alone. Measuring accuracy in this setting required more care than simple string matching. From an OpenAI agent unexpectedly breaching containment during security evaluations and infiltrating Hugging Face's production environment, to automated vulnerability mining lowering the barrier to zero-day exploitation to civilian levels, AI is arming both attackers and defenders with profoundly asymmetrical efficiency. The placement of this content is part of a paid service.*** | # PointGuard AI Launches AI Gateway to Secure Enterprise AI at Scale Distributed by EIN Presswire *Unified model routing, MCP security, and cost governance help enterprises control AI access, protect data, and manage spending* **We built AI Gateway so enterprises can scale AI with security controls in place, maintain performance, and keep spending accountable.”** — Pravin Kothari, CEO of PointGuard AI SAN JOSE, CA, UNITED STATES, October 29, 2026 /[EINPresswire.com](https://www.einpresswire.com/)/ — [PointGuard AI](https://www.pointguardai.com) today announced its [AI Gateway](https://www.pointguardai.com/ai-gateway), combining high-throughput model routing with AI-native security and cost governance. Integrated with the MCP Security Gateway, the solution helps enterprises block unapproved shadow models, protect sensitive data, contain runaway costs, and scale AI workloads across applications and agents. As agents connect to more models, tools, and enterprise resources, organizations need consistent controls over what AI can access and how it operates. In its Market Overview for AI Gateways, Gartner states, “AI gateways are essential components for managing how AI agents access both AI models and Model Context Protocol servers.”¹ “Every new model, agent, and tool connection introduces decisions about access, data, and cost,” said Pravin Kothari, founder and CEO of PointGuard AI. “We built AI Gateway so enterprises can scale AI with security controls in place, maintain performance, and keep spending accountable.” PointGuard AI Gateway brings together: • Approved model routing with automatic failover • Prompt guardrails and sensitive data protection • Semantic caching, virtual keys, and budgets • Identity-aware MCP tool authorization and inspection Its Java virtual-thread runtime delivered 50 times LiteLLM’s throughput in benchmark testing with thousands of concurrent requests. Hardened software builds and build provenance strengthen supply chain security, while unified LLM and MCP controls govern north-south and east-west AI traffic. Correlated telemetry connects usage, cost, identity, and security events for operational oversight. About PointGuard AI PointGuard AI is a Silicon Valley company providing comprehensive AI and application security and governance. Its platform helps enterprises discover AI assets, assess risk, test applications and agents, protect sensitive data, and enforce runtime policies across models, endpoints, MCP connections, and enterprise tools. Founded by industry veterans who previously built ArcSight, CipherCloud, and RiskVision, PointGuard AI brings deep expertise in cloud security, data protection, and risk management. PointGuard AI helps organizations adopt AI with the visibility, governance, and control needed to manage emerging risks. Open Source AI.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. Open Source AI.content: SecurityBrief Australia - Technology news for CISOs & cybersecurity decision-makers [![SecurityBrief Australia logo](/brands/sb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![CrowdStrike uncovers China-linked AI cyber campaign](https://securitybrief.com.au/uploads/story/2026/10/30/global-network-map-central-hub-intrusion-arrows-office-buildings-data-centers-story-323039.webp) [AI](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/artificial-intelligence) [Cybersecurity](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/cybersecurity) [Agentic AI](https://securitybrief.com.au/tag/ai-agents) # CrowdStrike uncovers China-linked AI cyber campaign Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://securitybrief.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) CrowdStrike has uncovered a cyber espionage campaign by China-linked threat actor VAPOR PANDA, which used an agentic artificial intelligence framework to conduct simultaneous intrusions against more than 200 organisations worldwide. The campaign began on October 17, 2026, and involved ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI framework, alongside the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model (LLM) and a second commercial LLM. The operation targeted government institutions, pharmaceutical companies, semiconductor organisations, defence entities and telecommunications providers. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller directed against organisations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day period. The activity included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as US-based organisations in several strategic industries. The cybersecurity company confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organisations, where the attackers gained access, deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and conducted further credential spraying, network scanning and reconnaissance. At least 12 additional organisations were subjected to password-spraying and credential-scanning activity, including US think tanks and European government entities. **Broad targeting** VAPOR PANDA conducted extensive intrusions against foreign ministries in two Latin American countries and likely compromised a third. The group also prepared target files for foreign ministries in Central America and Asia. In the Middle East, the adversary compromised an interior ministry. Another operation focused on a European country, targeting its foreign ministry, presidency and prime minister's office, alongside defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities. The campaign also involved 19 US-based organisations across the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defence, nuclear and financial sectors. Telecommunications providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also compromised. The targeting represents an expansion of VAPOR PANDA's previous activities. Since 2021, the group has primarily focused on government, think tank, energy and extractive organisations across Europe, North America, Oceania and the UK to establish long-term access. The latest campaign marks its first observed use of AI-driven intrusion tooling and a broader focus on pharmaceutical, semiconductor, nuclear and defence organisations. **AI operations** VAPOR PANDA primarily operated ARTEX using DeepSeek, supplemented by a second subscription-based commercial LLM that CrowdStrike Intelligence could not identify. Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open Weight Models: 6 Families, 16 GB Entry Point [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 29, 2026 · 27 min read Most teams pick an open weight model by leaderboard rank and read the license last. That order costs them. A model that tops a chart but ships under bespoke terms can stall a procurement review for weeks, while a slightly weaker Apache 2.0 checkpoint clears legal in an afternoon. As of October 29, 2026, six families dominate the conversation: OpenAI’s gpt-oss, Google’s Gemma 4, Mistral’s Large 4, Alibaba’s Qwen, DeepSeek’s V4.1 line, and Meta’s Llama and Muse releases. Their terms differ far more than their parameter counts. Here is the core point. Open weight models publish trained parameters for download, but that is not the same as open source in the way software teams use the term, and the license decides what you can actually ship. The [deepset explainer on open-weight models and sovereign AI](https://www.deepset.ai/blog/open-source-llm-open-weight-models) covers the definitional split well. Applied to the field today, the split is stark: only four of the twelve model entries in our table below carry a license we could confirm as Apache 2.0 from primary sources. Parameter counts and API prices already get plenty of coverage, including our [DeepSeek vs Qwen vs Mistral comparison](https://shattered.io/deepseek-vs-qwen-vs-mistral-open-weight-models-2026/). License terms, hardware floors and release status decide the rest, and they move weekly. Mistral Large 4’s weights are due by the end of October. Qwen4 is still in training. DeepSeek swapped its Flash model on October 17 without changing the API alias. A team that locked in a choice weeks ago may already be working from stale assumptions. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Open Weight Models Actually Give You An open weight release hands you the trained parameters, usually as files on Hugging Face, and lets you run them on hardware you control. It rarely hands you the training data, the full training code, or the data-filtering recipe. That gap matters for audits, for reproducibility, and for any team that needs to answer where a model learned its behavior. You get a finished artifact, not a recipe. OpenAI’s help center states the practical shape of this clearly for gpt-oss. The weights are free to download, they are meant to run on infrastructure you control or through a hosting provider, and OpenAI does not serve them through its own API or inside ChatGPT. That last point trips up newcomers. An open weight model from a lab that also sells a hosted API is two products with two sets of terms, and the hosted one is not what you get when you download the files. Running the weights yourself buys four things that a hosted API cannot. First, data stays inside your boundary, which matters for regulated workloads. Second, you can pin a version and keep it for as long as you like, instead of waiting for a vendor to retire it. Third, you can fine-tune with your own tooling. OpenAI, for example, offers no fine-tuning for gpt-oss through its APIs, so teams use external tools and their own infrastructure. Fourth, your cost curve changes from per-token to per-GPU-hour, which favors steady, high-volume traffic. The price of those benefits is operational. You own uptime, security patching, quantization choices, evaluation, and the legal review. Supply chain hygiene lands on you too. Infra & Chips.content: ![]() ![Zacks](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/zacks--theme-light.svg) ![Zacks](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/zacks--theme-dark.svg) # Founder-Led Giants Redefining Technology and Global Market Growth ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/nvidia.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/dell.svg) ***An updated edition of the Sept. 4, 2026, article.*** Founders often play a pivotal role in shaping the strategic direction, corporate culture and long-term growth prospects of the businesses they establish. Their deep-rooted commitment and entrepreneurial vision often encourage them to embrace calculated risks, navigate challenges and explore opportunities that conventional management teams might overlook. As their leadership philosophies become embedded in business operations, founder-led companies can develop distinct competitive advantages that support sustainable growth. Currently, approximately 11% of large-cap U.S. companies are founder-led. Despite accounting for less than 5% of the S&P 500, founder-led businesses wield considerable influence over the broader market. Visionary entrepreneurs such as Elon Musk, Warren Buffett, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates have reshaped industries and built globally recognized enterprises. Companies such as **NVIDIA** NVDA, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Tesla, Alphabet and Netflix demonstrate the lasting impact of entrepreneurial leadership and innovation. Together, these businesses represent nearly 15% of the S&P 500's market capitalization, with technology companies accounting for a significant portion. Founder-driven businesses often emerge from innovative concepts designed to capitalize on technological advancements and evolving consumer needs. During their formative years, entrepreneurs frequently encounter investor skepticism and financing challenges, prompting them to rely on personal resources before securing external funding. Infra & Chips.content: ![The Motley Fool](https://g.foolcdn.com/misc-assets/logo-tmf-primary-1-magenta-purple-reversed.svg?_w=320) ![The Motley Fool](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Fmisc-assets%2Ftmf_holdingco_logo_stacked_magenta_royalpurple_rev.png&w=96&op=resize) **Nvidia** ([NVDA](/quote/nasdaq/nvda/) -1.05%) and **Advanced Micro Devices** ([AMD](/quote/nasdaq/amd/) -2.41%) are two of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. As big tech [invests hundreds of billions of dollars in data centers](https://www.fool.com/research/ai-companies-spending-on-data-centers/), demand for semiconductors continues to accelerate. However, another chipmaker could deliver even greater returns over the next several years: **Marvell Technology** ([MRVL](/quote/nasdaq/mrvl/) -14.29%). Interestingly, Nvidia CEO [Jensen Huang](https://www.fool.com/investing/how-to-invest/famous-investors/jensen-huang/) recognizes Marvell's potential. During the Computex conference in June, Huang called Marvell the next potential trillion-dollar company. Nvidia has even invested $2 billion in Marvell, reinforcing its confidence in the company. Now, Marvell is reportedly exploring an acquisition that could supercharge its position in the AI infrastructure market. Let's dig into what makes Marvell unique and assess why the stock could be a compelling buy for long-term investors. ![Marvell logo.](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Feditorial%2Fimages%2F892727%2Fmrvl.jpg&w=3840&op=resize) Image source: The Motley Fool. ## What role does Marvell play in the AI chip stack? Nvidia and AMD primarily design general-purpose AI accelerators, known as GPUs. Marvell specializes in designing [custom application-specific integrated circuits](https://www.fool.com/terms/a/application-specific-integrated-circuit/) (ASICs). These processors are tailored to specific workloads, potentially offering superior training and inference performance, energy efficiency, and economics compared with off-the-shelf chips. This value proposition appeals to hyperscalers such as **Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms**. Rather than relying exclusively on products from Nvidia and AMD, big tech is also investing in custom silicon designed around their own AI models. Marvell is positioning itself as a partner in this transition. Marvell's opportunity extends beyond custom chips. Its portfolio also includes optical digital signal processors (DSPs)**,** Ethernet switches, high-speed interconnects, and silicon photonics. These products help move data between larger clusters of GPUs and memory. As AI models evolve and use cases become more sophisticated, Marvell's services should see increased demand. ## Is Marvell acquiring Lumentum? On Oct. 28, Reuters reported that Marvell was in advanced discussions to acquire **Lumentum** ([LITE](/quote/nasdaq/lite/) +0.79%), a manufacturer of optical components used in telecommunications networks and AI data centers. Wall Street initially reacted negatively, as Marvell stock declined more than 8% following reports of the discussions. ## [MRVL](/quote/nasdaq/mrvl/) - Marvell Technology NASDAQ · As of 3:35 PM ET 10/29/26 ![](/jester-cap-color.svg) ### Key data points The concerns are understandable. At the end of its fiscal second quarter, Marvell held approximately $3.9 billion in cash on its balance sheet. Lumentum boasts a market capitalization of $84 billion, meaning that an acquisition of this magnitude would require substantial borrowing, additional share issuance, or some combination of both by Marvell. Even so, I see the strategic rationale here. One challenge facing AI data centers is moving information quickly and efficiently between large clusters of processors. Copper-based connections have limitations around bandwidth, distance, and power consumption. Infra & Chips.content: Updated : Friday, October 30, 2026, 10:21 * [Home](/) * [Login](https://www.businesskorea.co.kr/member/login.html) * [Sign in](https://www.businesskorea.co.kr/member/index.html) * [Korean](/?editcode=MAIN_13) [![Businesskorea](/image/logo/toplogo_20230426040837.png) ![](/image/logo/year_40.png)](/) [![Businesskorea](/image/logo/printlogo_20230426040837.png)](https://www.businesskorea.co.kr) Nvidia to Become Naver's Third-Largest Shareholder With $1 Billion Investment Scroll Move Status-bar # Nvidia to Become Naver's Third-Largest Shareholder With $1 Billion Investment * *Editor* Park Jung-hwan * 2026.10.30 10:10 ## Strategic Investment to Accelerate $9 billion AI Infrastructure Partnership with Brookfield ![Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang poses with Naver Chairman Lee Hae-jin during a visit to Naver's 1784 headquarters in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province, on June 8.](/news/photo/202610/280046_287820_93.jpg) Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang poses with Naver Chairman Lee Hae-jin during a visit to Naver's 1784 headquarters in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province, on June 8. Naver is set to receive a $1 billion investment, approximately 1.35 trillion won, from U.S. AI chip giant Nvidia, establishing a strategic alliance aimed at expanding its presence in the global artificial intelligence market. Upon completion of the investment, Nvidia is expected to become Naver's third-largest shareholder, behind the National Pension Service and BlackRock. Naver said in an amended regulatory filing on Oct. 30 that the payment date for Nvidia's investment had been set for Nov. 6. The payment deadline was pushed back one week from Oct. 30, while the scheduled listing date for the new shares was moved from Nov. 20 to Nov. 27. The final number of shares to be issued and the investment amount in Korean won will be determined using the average exchange rate published by Seoul Money Brokerage Services on Nov. 3. The investment follows a share subscription agreement signed by Naver and Nvidia in July. The issue price has been set at 204,500 won per share, with a provisional issuance of 7,241,564 shares and expected proceeds of approximately 1.4809 trillion won. These preliminary figures are based on an exchange rate of 1,480.9 won per dollar, meaning the final issuance size will depend on the exchange rate applied. Naver has also fulfilled a key prerequisite for the investment by securing at least $9 billion, approximately 12.15 trillion won, in computing infrastructure, excluding proceeds from the share issuance. The infrastructure will form a core part of the global AI factory project jointly pursued by Naver, Nvidia and Brookfield. On Oct. 27, Naver signed a computing infrastructure agreement with Brookfield. Under the arrangement, Brookfield will invest in infrastructure, including graphics processing units (GPUs) and data centers, through a special purpose vehicle (SPV), while Naver Cloud will use those resources to provide AI computing services. Nvidia is expected to provide technology support centered on its next-generation AI infrastructure platform, DSX. Nvidia is expected to acquire an approximately 4.54% stake in Naver, reshaping the company's shareholder structure. As of August, the National Pension Service was Naver's largest shareholder with a 9.49% stake, followed by BlackRock with 7.31%. Founder and board chairman Lee Hae-jin, currently the third-largest shareholder, is expected to see his stake diluted from 4.03% to approximately 3.84%, moving him down one place in the shareholder rankings. However, the final ownership percentages of both Nvidia and Lee may vary depending on the confirmed number of newly issued shares. Nvidia's shares will be electronically registered with the Korea Securities Depository and subject to a one-year lock-up period following registration, during which they cannot be withdrawn or sold. Lee's decision to welcome Nvidia as a strategic shareholder despite the dilution of his own stake reflects his longstanding emphasis on business expansio...

Infra & Chips.titleZh: The many types of AI chips on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure - Techzine Global
Infra & Chips.content: A wide variety of AI chips will be available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). In addition to variants of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin architecture, Google TPUs will be available for the first time starting next year; the same applies to the large Cerebras chips. AMD, Intel, SambaNova, and OpenAI Jalapeño are expected to follow, though it is not yet known when. Oracle unveiled a long list of hardware announcements at AI World in Las Vegas. Nvidia discusses credit guarantees for Nscale’s deal with Anthropic — Channel NewsAsia [Fedir Kryshtovskyi](/en/%D0%A4%D0%B5%D0%B4%D1%96%D1%80%20%D0%9A%D1%80%D0%B8%D1%88%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B2%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9) 30 October 2026 03:37 ![Nvidia discusses credit guarantees for Nscale’s deal with Anthropic — Channel NewsAsia](https://cdn-cabinet.ua.news/uploads/images/nvidia_credit_guarantees_nscale_anthropi_1793324252559.webp?8075097 "Nvidia discusses credit guarantees for Nscale’s deal with Anthropic — Channel NewsAsia") Nvidia is in talks to provide the cloud AI services supplier Nscale with multibillion-dollar credit guarantees to support debt financing for a data center in the US state of West Virginia that Anthropic plans to use. [Channel NewsAsia](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/business/nvidia-in-talks-give-credit-support-nscales-deal-anthropic-information-reports-6505526) reported this, citing Reuters, which cited The Information and sources familiar with the negotiations. ## Data center financing According to The Information, Nvidia’s credit support is intended to help finance the energy infrastructure and construction of Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia. Nvidia is an investor in the British cloud provider Nscale. The deal has not yet been signed, and its terms may change. Nvidia, Nscale and Anthropic did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on the information. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel [Telegram](https://telegram.me/uanewsstream). ## Agreements with Anthropic In August, Anthropic, the developer of Claude, entered into an agreement to spend $45 billion on leasing computing capacity at Nscale’s data center campus in West Virginia. Nscale is also in talks to sell Anthropic about 460 megawatts of AI computing capacity in another deal, whose value could also be about $45 billion. The report comes amid concerns over debt financing for the expansion of AI infrastructure. Such concerns have affected Coreweave and Firmus, which also have Nvidia’s backing.
